families.name: Punk and making their own rules

genres.name: Mamie Smith: Crazy Blues
genres.text: On 10 August 1920, Mamie Smith recorded Crazy Blues in New York, the first blues record by a Black woman singer. In the first month alone it sold some 75,000 copies. Record companies suddenly understood that there was a Black audience that wanted to buy records. They started separate series for that audience: race records. In the first half of the 1920s, the biggest blues stars were women.
genres.listen: Listen to the horns and the piano behind Mamie Smith: this is not porch guitar blues, but city blues from the theatre.

genres.name: Women's suffrage in America
genres.text: On 18 August 1920, Tennessee became the last state needed to ratify a constitutional amendment giving American women the right to vote. In the South, Black women, like Black men, still could not vote in practice for decades. In that very same month, a Black woman singer in New York recorded a song that would change the music industry.

genres.name: Bessie Smith: Downhearted Blues
genres.text: On 16 February 1923, Bessie Smith from Chattanooga recorded Downhearted Blues in New York. The record sold some 780,000 copies in half a year and became one of the first big hits for the record company Columbia. Smith became the best-paid Black performer of the 1920s, the Empress of the Blues. She did not sing politely, but about money, drink, unfaithful men and women who could manage on their own.
genres.listen: There was no electric microphone yet: the band stood in front of a big horn. Listen to how Smith has to sing loudly and precisely, as if in a tent without amplification.

genres.name: Ma Rainey
genres.text: At the end of 1923, Ma Rainey recorded her first records for the Paramount label in Chicago. She had been performing for twenty years in travelling tent shows across the South and was known as the Mother of the Blues. She wore gold necklaces and sang openly about love for women. The teenage Bessie Smith performed in the same travelling show around 1912. Rainey's records brought the blues from the South to the cities.
genres.listen: See See Rider Blues from 1924 became one of her best-known songs. Listen to the jazz band behind her and her low, heavy voice.

genres.name: Lil Hardin Armstrong
genres.text: Lil Hardin was a pianist, composer and bandleader in Chicago. In 1924 she married the trumpeter Louis Armstrong and pushed him to go his own way. On 12 November 1925 she recorded the first records of his Hot Five with him, playing piano. She also wrote songs for the group. In the history books, Louis mostly got the credit; Lil stayed in his shadow for a long time.
genres.listen: Lil Hardin wrote Struttin' with Some Barbecue from 1927. Listen to Louis's trumpet and her piano, which carries the rhythm.

tracks.artist: Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five
tracks.title: Struttin' with Some Barbecue

genres.name: Memphis Minnie: When the Levee Breaks
genres.text: On 18 June 1929, Memphis Minnie recorded When the Levee Breaks in New York with her husband Kansas Joe McCoy. The song is about the great Mississippi flood of 1927, when levees broke and hundreds of thousands of people lost their homes. Minnie was one of the few women in the blues who played guitar herself, and she played it as well as the men.
genres.listen: Listen to the two guitars playing around each other: Minnie and Joe take turns with short runs.

genres.name: The Andrews Sisters: Bei Mir Bist Du Schön
genres.text: On 24 November 1937, the sisters LaVerne, Maxene and Patty Andrews recorded Bei Mir Bist Du Schön, a Yiddish song from a theatre in Brooklyn, with new English words. Within a month a quarter of a million records had been sold and the three sisters were famous. Their tight close harmony, in which the voices lie very close together, became a model for later girl groups.
genres.listen: Listen to how the three voices sound almost like one instrument, and how a few Yiddish words have stayed in the song.

genres.name: Ella Fitzgerald: A-Tisket, A-Tasket
genres.text: On 2 May 1938, the 21-year-old Ella Fitzgerald recorded A-Tisket, A-Tasket with drummer Chick Webb's orchestra. She had turned an old nursery rhyme into a swinging jazz song herself, together with arranger Al Feldman. The record became a number one hit. Fitzgerald grew into the First Lady of Song, known for her pure voice and for scat: singing with sounds instead of words.
genres.listen: Listen to how Ella makes the simple nursery rhyme swing, with the big band answering briefly each time.

genres.name: Billie Holiday: Strange Fruit
genres.text: On 20 April 1939, Billie Holiday recorded Strange Fruit, a song about the lynching of Black Americans in the South. The words came from a poem by the teacher Abel Meeropol. Her own record company did not dare to release it, so a small label did. Holiday sang it at the end of her performances, with the lights off except for one spotlight. It is regarded as one of the first great protest songs.
genres.listen: Listen to how slow and bare the song is. Holiday sings the horrifying words almost without showing emotion, and that is exactly what makes it so hard-hitting.

genres.name: Sister Rosetta Tharpe
genres.text: In 1944, Sister Rosetta Tharpe recorded Strange Things Happening Every Day with pianist Sammy Price. It is a gospel song, but you hear a driving piano, a voice full of energy and an electric guitar solo. It was the first gospel record in the chart for Black music. Elvis, Little Richard and Chuck Berry named her as an influence. She is called the godmother of rock 'n' roll and entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.
genres.listen: Listen for the guitar solo in the middle: ten years before the word rock 'n' roll became common, a woman from the church was already playing it.

genres.name: Mahalia Jackson: Move On Up a Little Higher
genres.text: On 12 September 1947, Mahalia Jackson recorded Move On Up a Little Higher in New York, a gospel song by Reverend William Herbert Brewster. Millions of copies were sold, more than of any other gospel record. Jackson sang only religious music and refused to sing the blues. Later she sang at civil rights gatherings, including in 1963 in Washington, just before Martin Luther King's famous speech.
genres.listen: Listen to how Jackson stretches and decorates the long notes, and how the song grows fiercer and higher.

tracks.title: Move On Up a Little Higher

genres.name: Ruth Brown: Teardrops from My Eyes
genres.text: In October 1950, Ruth Brown's Teardrops from My Eyes was released. It spent eleven weeks at number one in the R&B chart, the chart for Black music. Her hits made the small label Atlantic so big that it got a nickname: the house that Ruth built. Brown herself later saw little of that money. That is why she fought in the 1980s for fair royalties, the money artists receive for each record sold.
genres.listen: Listen to Brown's danceable rhythm and clear voice: the rhythm and blues from which rock 'n' roll grew a few years later.

genres.name: Kitty Wells: Honky Tonk Angels
genres.text: On 3 May 1952, Kitty Wells recorded It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels in Nashville. It was an answer to a Hank Thompson hit that blamed women for infidelity. Wells sings that it is men who lead women astray. NBC banned the song from the radio, but it became the first number one hit by a woman singing alone in the American country chart.
genres.listen: Listen to the weeping steel guitar and Wells's calm, almost dry voice, which makes its point without drama.

tracks.title: It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels

genres.name: Big Mama Thornton: Hound Dog
genres.text: On 13 August 1952, Big Mama Thornton recorded Hound Dog in Los Angeles. It became a big hit in 1953: seven weeks at number one in the chart for Black music. You hear a dragging rhythm, a voice that mocks, growls and lashes out, and a woman who is the boss in the relationship. Three years later Elvis made it a worldwide hit. Thornton received about 500 dollars for her own version.
genres.listen: Compare Thornton with Elvis: in hers it is about a man who lives off her, in his about a dog that never caught a rabbit.

genres.name: Mickey & Sylvia: Love Is Strange
genres.text: At the beginning of 1957, Mickey & Sylvia had a hit with Love Is Strange. Sylvia Vanderpool sang and played guitar, which was unusual for a woman in rhythm and blues. The conversation between the two halfway through became famous. Later she married Joe Robinson and became Sylvia Robinson: singer, producer and owner of record labels. Twenty years later she would put hip-hop on record.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar riff at the start and the spoken part in the middle, in which Mickey asks how Sylvia calls her lover and she gives the answer.

genres.name: Daphne Oram and the Radiophonic Workshop
genres.text: In April 1958, the BBC started the Radiophonic Workshop, a studio for electronic sounds for radio and television. Daphne Oram had fought for it for years and became its first head. A year later she left and started her own studio in Kent. There she built Oramics, a machine on which you draw music onto strips of film. A remarkable number of the pioneers of electronic music were women, but they rarely made it into the books.

genres.name: Wanda Jackson, queen of rockabilly
genres.text: Wanda Jackson from Oklahoma toured with Elvis Presley in 1955 and 1956, and he advised her to start singing rock 'n' roll. At the end of 1957, Fujiyama Mama came out, with a raw, growling voice that nobody expected from a girl. In America almost nobody wanted to play it, but in Japan it was at number one for months in 1958. She was called the Queen of Rockabilly, but her rock songs hardly became hits in America.
genres.listen: Listen to how Jackson growls and screams in Fujiyama Mama, just as wild as the men of rock 'n' roll.

genres.name: The Shirelles and Carole King
genres.text: On 30 January 1961, Will You Love Me Tomorrow by The Shirelles was at number one in America, as one of the first songs by a Black girl group to get there. The group came from a high school in New Jersey. The song was written by the eighteen-year-old Carole King and her husband Gerry Goffin, in a small office in New York where writers turned out hits for others as if in a factory.
genres.listen: The girl asks whether the boy will still love her tomorrow. Listen to the strings and the soft backing vocals: an honest question in a pop song.

genres.name: Patsy Cline: Crazy
genres.text: On 16 October 1961, Patsy Cline's Crazy was released, written by the then unknown Willie Nelson. Cline had recently had a serious car accident and at first could not reach the high notes. Weeks later she sang the song in a single take. Crazy became a hit in both the country and the pop chart. Cline showed that country women singers could also reach the general public.
genres.listen: Listen to how Cline stretches the words and lets them falter, as if she herself cannot believe what she feels.

genres.name: Anneke Grönloh: Brandend zand
genres.text: In July 1962, Brandend zand by Anneke Grönloh was released, a Dutch version of a German hit. The song spent two weeks at number one and about a million copies were sold in the Netherlands, an enormous number for that time. Grönloh, born in Indonesia, became one of the biggest stars in the country. In 2010 the song was at number three in the Evergreen Top 1000.
genres.listen: Listen to Grönloh's warm, slightly dark voice and the chorus that everyone could sing along to.

genres.name: Ellie Greenwich and Be My Baby
genres.text: In the summer of 1963, Be My Baby by The Ronettes was released, with singer Ronnie Bennett. The song was written by Ellie Greenwich, her husband Jeff Barry and producer Phil Spector. Greenwich wrote many hits for girl groups. Spector built a wall of sound in the studio and received most of the credit. Ronnie later married him and told years later that he had kept her prisoner at home.
genres.listen: Listen to the famous drum beat at the start: boom, boom-boom, smack. Then comes the wall of sound with strings, castanets and backing vocals.

genres.name: Delia Derbyshire: Doctor Who
genres.text: On 23 November 1963, the first episode of Doctor Who was broadcast. The theme tune was written by Ron Grainer, but Delia Derbyshire of the Radiophonic Workshop turned it into sound. No band plays: the melody comes from oscillators, the bass from the recording of a single plucked string, and every note is a piece of cut-and-spliced tape. Grainer wanted to name her as co-composer, but the BBC did not allow it.
genres.listen: Listen to the humming bass and the floating melody. Everything was put together by hand, piece of tape by piece of tape.

genres.name: Tharpe at a station in Manchester
genres.text: On 7 May 1964, Sister Rosetta Tharpe played at a deserted railway station in Manchester, for a television programme about blues and gospel. It was raining, she arrived in a horse-drawn carriage and played in a coat with an electric guitar. Among the young Britons in the audience and in front of the television were musicians who later became famous. That is how her guitar playing reached the British rock bands of the 1960s.
genres.listen: In Didn't It Rain she sings about the flood, while in Manchester it was really raining. Listen to her fast electric guitar.

genres.name: Aretha Franklin: Respect
genres.text: On 10 April 1967, Respect by Aretha Franklin was released, a song by Otis Redding. With her sisters Carolyn and Erma she added the spelled-out R-E-S-P-E-C-T and the sock it to me, and she played piano herself. Aretha was singer and arranger at once. Otis Redding later said that a girl had taken his song. It became a song for the civil rights movement and for the women's movement.
genres.listen: Listen for the stop-time: the band falls silent for a moment so that only the voice remains. Hear how the sisters keep answering.

genres.name: Janis Joplin: Piece of My Heart
genres.text: In 1968, Janis Joplin turned Piece of My Heart into a rock song with Big Brother & the Holding Company; Erma Franklin, Aretha's sister, had recorded it a year earlier. Joplin did not sing prettily and with restraint, as was expected of women singers. She screamed, cracked and lashed out, like her great example Big Mama Thornton. In 1970 she helped pay for a gravestone for Bessie Smith. Two months later she died, aged 27.
genres.listen: Listen to the raw outbursts in the chorus and the tearing guitars. The line runs from Bessie Smith via Thornton to Joplin.

tracks.artist: Big Brother & The Holding Company & Janis Joplin
tracks.title: Piece of My Heart

genres.name: Wendy Carlos: Switched-On Bach
genres.text: In October 1968, Switched-On Bach by Wendy Carlos was released, who had worked closely with Robert Moog on his synthesizer. The Moog could play only one note at a time, so Carlos recorded each voice separately and layered the recordings. The album was a great success and won three Grammys. It showed a wide audience that a synthesizer was an instrument. In 1979 Carlos said that she is a trans woman.

genres.name: Lenny Kuhr wins the Eurovision Song Contest
genres.text: On 29 March 1969, Lenny Kuhr won the Eurovision Song Contest in Madrid with De troubadour. She had written the music herself; the words came from David Hartsema. That evening four countries tied for first place, something that never happened before or since. Kuhr was a young singer with a guitar, a songwriter in a world where women singers mostly sang other people's songs.
genres.listen: Listen to how the song begins like an old story and then grows with the orchestra.

genres.name: Shocking Blue: Venus
genres.text: On 7 February 1970, Venus by the band Shocking Blue from The Hague was at number one in America, the first Dutch number one there. Singer Mariska Veres, with long black hair and a dark voice, became the face of the band. Guitarist Robbie van Leeuwen wrote the song. Sixteen years later the British girl group Bananarama made it a worldwide hit again.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar riff at the start and the low voice of Mariska Veres, which sounds a bit like English with an accent.

genres.name: Carole King: Tapestry
genres.text: On 10 February 1971, Tapestry by Carole King was released; she had spent ten years writing hits for others. Now she sang her songs herself, with her own piano as the basis. The album became one of the best-selling of the 1970s. King belonged to the singer-songwriters, who wrote in the first person about their own lives. Like Joni Mitchell, she showed that a woman could write her own album.
genres.listen: In It's Too Late you hear soft, wistful chords from soul and jazz. The words about a relationship that is over were written by Toni Stern.

genres.name: Joni Mitchell: Blue
genres.text: On 22 June 1971, Blue by the Canadian Joni Mitchell was released, an album full of personal songs about love, travel and doubt. It is regarded as the model of the confessional album, like reading a diary. Mitchell tuned her guitar in dozens of different open tunings, which produced chords that other guitarists did not easily play. Later in the 1970s she moved more and more towards jazz.
genres.listen: She wrote Both Sides Now in 1967. She recorded it again in 2000 with an orchestra. Listen to how different a song about looking back sounds with an older voice.

genres.name: Helen Reddy: I Am Woman
genres.text: On 9 December 1972, I Am Woman by the Australian singer Helen Reddy was at number one in America. She wrote the words herself, because she could not find songs about how she felt as a woman. The song became the anthem of the women's movement of the 1970s. When she received her Grammy, Reddy thanked God, because He made everything possible.
genres.listen: The chorus is a statement: I am strong, I am invincible, I am woman. Listen to how the song builds up to that chorus.

genres.name: Sylvia: Pillow Talk
genres.text: In the spring of 1973, Sylvia Robinson had a hit under the name Sylvia with Pillow Talk, a sultry soul song with whispered and sighed vocals. She had actually written it for Al Green, but he thought it too daring. With her husband she had her own record label and studio in Englewood, New Jersey. There she would make history a few years later.
genres.listen: Listen to the whispers and sighs above the soft soul groove. Six years later the same Sylvia produced Rapper's Delight.

genres.name: Dolly Parton says no to Elvis
genres.text: In 1973, Dolly Parton wrote I Will Always Love You, as a farewell to her mentor Porter Wagoner. When it became a country hit in 1974, Elvis Presley wanted to record it, but his manager demanded half of the rights. Parton refused. In 1992 Whitney Houston recorded it for the film The Bodyguard. It became one of the best-selling singles ever, and Parton earned millions from it, because she had kept her rights.
genres.listen: Compare Dolly's soft country version with Whitney Houston's big vocal flight: the same song, two worlds.

genres.name: Teach-In wins the Eurovision Song Contest
genres.text: On 22 March 1975, the Dutch group Teach-In won the Eurovision Song Contest in Stockholm with Ding-a-dong, sung by Getty Kaspers. It was the fourth Dutch victory, and the last until 2019. The song became a hit all over Europe. Kaspers stood at the front of a group of men, as often happened in those years: the woman singer as the face, the men behind the instruments.
genres.listen: Ding-a-dong is a cheerful, skipping pop song. Listen to how the chorus is made to be sung along to in any language.

genres.name: Patti Smith: Horses
genres.text: On 10 November 1975, Horses was released, the first album by the poet Patti Smith from New York. She performed at the club CBGB, where the Ramones and Television also played. On the cover she wears a white shirt with a jacket over her shoulder, without make-up: not how a pop singer was supposed to look. Her mix of poetry and raw rock made her one of the founders of punk.
genres.listen: Gloria begins with the famous line that Jesus died for somebody's sins, but not for hers. Then it turns into a rock song by Them.

genres.name: The Runaways
genres.text: In 1976, the first album by The Runaways was released, a rock band of five teenage girls from Los Angeles, with Joan Jett and Lita Ford on guitar and Cherie Currie as singer. Their manager put the band together and shaped much of their image, including the corsets that Currie wore. They became big in Japan. Joan Jett later became a star with I Love Rock 'n' Roll and started her own label.
genres.listen: Cherry Bomb revolves around the shouted chorus. Listen to the hard guitars: girls who played just as loudly as boy bands.

genres.name: X-Ray Spex: Oh Bondage Up Yours!
genres.text: On 30 September 1977, Oh Bondage Up Yours!, the first single by X-Ray Spex, was released. Singer Poly Styrene wrote it after a Sex Pistols gig. She opens with the words that some people think girls should be seen and not heard, and then screams it out. With her braces and bright clothes she fitted no ideal of beauty, and that was exactly the point.
genres.listen: Listen to the soft beginning and then the eruption: Poly screams and the saxophone shrieks along.

genres.name: Kate Bush: Wuthering Heights
genres.text: On 11 March 1978, Wuthering Heights by the nineteen-year-old Kate Bush was at number one in England. She had written it herself, after the novel by Emily Brontë. That made her the first woman in Great Britain with a self-written number one. Her record company wanted another song as the first single, but Bush held out. From the start she wanted to decide for herself how her music sounded.
genres.listen: Listen to the high, theatrical voice. Bush sings like Cathy's ghost knocking at the window, from Brontë's novel.

genres.name: Blondie: Heart of Glass
genres.text: On 28 April 1979, Heart of Glass by Blondie was at number one in America. Singer Debbie Harry came from the punk scene of CBGB, but this song was disco, with a drum machine and synthesizers. Punk fans saw it as betrayal. Harry became a style icon, with bleached hair and a cool gaze. She wrote the song with guitarist Chris Stein. Blondie showed that punk, disco and pop could go together.
genres.listen: Listen to the ticking drum machine and the floating synthesizers. Harry sings high and aloof, like an icy disco diva.

genres.name: The Slits: Cut
genres.text: On 7 September 1979, Cut was released, the first album by The Slits, a punk band of women from London. Producer Dennis Bovell brought reggae and dub into their music: lots of space, heavy bass and echo. In Typical Girls they laugh at everything expected of an ordinary girl, such as worrying about your looks. The band played clumsily but stubbornly, and that made them special.
genres.listen: In Typical Girls, listen to the bouncing bass and the shrill voice of Ari Up, who ridicules the expectations placed on girls.

genres.name: Sylvia Robinson puts hip-hop on record
genres.text: In 1979, Sylvia Robinson and her husband founded Sugar Hill Records. At the club Harlem World she heard young people rapping over music, and she put together a group herself, the Sugarhill Gang. In September 1979 she produced Rapper's Delight, the first hip-hop record to become a hit. She is sometimes called the Mother of Hip-Hop, but in most stories about the beginning of hip-hop she stays in the margins.
genres.listen: In its long version, Rapper's Delight lasts almost a quarter of an hour, over the bass line of Chic's Good Times, replayed by a studio band.

genres.name: Tina Turner: Private Dancer
genres.text: In 1976, Tina Turner fled from her husband and bandleader Ike Turner, with almost no money. For years she had suffered his violence. In the divorce she wanted to keep only her stage name. On 29 May 1984, Private Dancer was released, and What's Love Got to Do with It became her first number one. She was 44, old for a pop star. It became one of the biggest comebacks in pop music.
genres.listen: In What's Love Got to Do with It, Turner asks what love has to do with it. Listen to her hoarse, powerful voice above the cool synthesizers.

tracks.title: What's Love Got to Do with It

genres.name: Roxanne Shanté
genres.text: At the end of 1984, the teenager Lolita Gooden from Queensbridge in New York recorded Roxanne's Revenge, as an answer to a rap song by UTFO about a girl who was not interested in boys. She rapped it in one take, without writing anything down. As Roxanne Shanté she became famous. Dozens of answer records by others followed, the Roxanne Wars. A teenage girl had shown that she could rap just as sharply as the boys.
genres.listen: Listen to how fast and cheeky Shanté raps, over a beat she borrowed from the UTFO song.

genres.name: Kate Bush: Hounds of Love
genres.text: On 16 September 1985, Hounds of Love by Kate Bush was released. She had recorded it in her own studio next to her house, so that she could work without a record company looking over her shoulder, and she produced it herself. She used the Fairlight, a computer on which you can play any recorded sound on a keyboard. Running Up That Hill is about the wish to swap places with a lover.
genres.listen: Running Up That Hill consists of few parts: a drum machine, a sustained sound from the Fairlight and her voice in layers.

genres.name: Salt-N-Pepa: Push It
genres.text: In 1987, Push It by Salt-N-Pepa was released, two rappers from Queens with DJ Spinderella. The song was first a B-side, until DJs began to play it in clubs. In 1988 it became a worldwide hit. Salt-N-Pepa became one of the first female rap groups with platinum records. In Let's Talk About Sex from 1991 they rapped openly about sex and safety. They showed that women in hip-hop could talk about their own bodies.
genres.listen: Listen to the squealing synthesizer and the endlessly repeated push it. The song is made for the dance floor.

genres.name: Queen Latifah: Ladies First
genres.text: In November 1989, Ladies First by Queen Latifah from New Jersey was released, with the British rapper Monie Love. The song is a feminist statement: women in hip-hop are not the backdrop, but come first. In the video you see images of Black women from history, such as Sojourner Truth and Angela Davis, and a map of South Africa. Latifah later also became an actress and producer.
genres.listen: Listen to how the two rappers alternate, with an American and a British accent, over a tight beat.

genres.name: Riot grrrl
genres.text: On 20 August 1991, a week of punk concerts began in Olympia, Washington, with a first evening on which only women played. Bands such as Bikini Kill, with singer Kathleen Hanna, and Bratmobile felt that the punk scene had become a man's world. They made their own fanzines, small labels and rules, and called themselves riot grrrl. Hanna once wrote on Kurt Cobain's wall that he smelled like Teen Spirit.
genres.listen: Rebel Girl by Bikini Kill from 1993 has three chords, a hard drum and words about a girl whom Hanna admires for her nerve.

genres.name: Madonna's own label
genres.text: In April 1992, Madonna signed a contract with Time Warner that gave her her own company, Maverick, with a record label, a film division and a publishing house. The contract was worth tens of millions of dollars. Madonna was not a singer made by a label, but a businesswoman with her own label. Maverick later released, among others, Alanis Morissette, whose Jagged Little Pill sold tens of millions of copies worldwide in 1995.
genres.listen: Vogue from 1990 is about voguing, a dance from the Black and Latino gay clubs of New York. Madonna brought it to the charts.

genres.name: Whitney Houston: I Will Always Love You
genres.text: In November 1992, I Will Always Love You by Whitney Houston was released, from the film The Bodyguard. The song begins without accompaniment, only her voice, and bursts open towards the end after one hit on the drums. It spent fourteen weeks at number one in America and became one of the best-selling singles ever. The writer of the song, Dolly Parton, made a fortune from it, because she had kept her rights.
genres.listen: Listen to the opening without a band: only a voice. Wait for the hit on the drums towards the end, after which the song breaks loose.

genres.name: Björk: Post
genres.text: In June 1995, Post by the Icelandic Björk was released. She writes, arranges and produces her albums herself, together with a changing cast of producers. Hyperballad combines strings with a beat from rave and techno. Still, journalists often attributed her music to the men she worked with. A woman who sings is seen as a singer; that she also sits at the computer is easily overlooked.
genres.listen: Hyperballad is about someone who throws things off a cliff early every morning, to then calmly go back to her lover. Listen to strings and rave beat together.

genres.name: Anouk: Nobody's Wife
genres.text: In 1997, Anouk from The Hague broke through with Nobody's Wife, a rock song in English. It became a big hit and is still often played on the radio. Anouk sang rawly and with confidence, and said what she thought in interviews and on stage. In 2013 she brought the Netherlands back to the Eurovision final with Birds for the first time in nine years.
genres.listen: Listen to the chorus, which sounds like a statement: I am nobody's wife. A Dutch rock hit, raw and loud.

genres.name: Lilith Fair
genres.text: On 5 July 1997, Lilith Fair began in George, Washington, a touring festival with only women artists. The Canadian singer Sarah McLachlan came up with it, after radio stations and concert organisers had said that you could not play or book two women in a row. The festival became one of the best-attended tours of the summer and showed that this prejudice was wrong.
genres.listen: McLachlan's Building a Mystery from 1997 became a big hit, even eight weeks at number one in Canada. Listen to the soft guitar and her clear voice.

genres.name: Lauryn Hill: The Miseducation
genres.text: On 25 August 1998, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill was released, the only studio album by the singer and rapper of The Fugees. She wrote, sang, rapped and produced it. In 1999 it won five Grammys, including album of the year, as the first hip-hop album. A conflict did arise over the credits: musicians who had contributed felt they were credited too little. The case was settled.
genres.listen: Doo Wop (That Thing) combines backing vocals from the doo-wop of the 1950s with horns and a rap. Hill warns women and men alike.

genres.name: Missy Elliott: Get Ur Freak On
genres.text: In March 2001, Get Ur Freak On by Missy Elliott from Portsmouth, Virginia, was released. She first wrote songs for others, including Aaliyah, and from 1997 made her own albums with her childhood friend, producer Timbaland. She co-wrote and co-produced, and her videos with strange costumes were unlike anything in hip-hop. In 2019 she became the first female rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.
genres.listen: The song revolves around a short motif on the tumbi, a one-string lute from Punjab, with tablas and a Japanese exclamation at the start.

genres.name: Within Temptation
genres.text: At the beginning of 2002, Ice Queen by Within Temptation from Waddinxveen became a big hit in the Netherlands and Belgium. The band of singer Sharon den Adel and guitarist Robert Westerholt made symphonic metal: heavy guitars with orchestral sounds and a clear, high voice. Together with Nightwish from Finland it became one of the best-known bands in the genre, which often had a woman as singer. They later played at festivals all over the world.
genres.listen: Listen to the contrast in Ice Queen: heavy metal guitars and a choir, with the pure voice of Sharon den Adel above them.

genres.name: Imogen Heap: Speak for Yourself
genres.text: On 18 July 2005, Imogen Heap released Speak for Yourself on her own label. No bank wanted to lend her money, so she took out an extra mortgage on her house. She wrote, played, produced and mixed almost everything herself in her home studio. She sang the song Hide and Seek through a harmonizer, a device that turns one voice into a choir. Through the TV series The O.C. the song became world famous.
genres.listen: In Hide and Seek you hear only Heap's voice, turned by the harmonizer into an electronic choir without other instruments.

genres.name: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black
genres.text: On 27 October 2006, Back to Black by Amy Winehouse was released. Producers Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi gave the album the sound of 1960s girl groups and soul, with the band The Dap-Kings from Brooklyn. Winehouse wrote honest, sometimes raw lyrics about love and addiction. The album won Grammys and sold some twenty million copies worldwide. In 2011 she died, aged 27.
genres.listen: In Back to Black, listen to the echoing piano and drums from the 1960s, with Winehouse's low, lived-in voice over them.

genres.name: Lady Gaga: The Fame
genres.text: On 19 August 2008, The Fame was released, the first album by Lady Gaga from New York. She co-wrote every song. She made Just Dance in about ten minutes with producer RedOne. It took the song 22 weeks to reach number one in America. Gaga combined dance music with striking costumes and videos, and made fame itself the subject of her art.
genres.listen: Listen to the synthesizers and the tight dance beat, and how the chorus sticks right away.

genres.name: Adele: 21
genres.text: On 24 January 2011, 21 by Adele from London was released, on the small independent label XL. She wrote the songs about a broken relationship, with help from writers such as Paul Epworth. With more than thirty million copies it became the best-selling album of this century. It spent 23 weeks at number one in England and 24 weeks in America, and won six Grammys.
genres.listen: In Rolling in the Deep, listen to the stamping beat and guitar, and how Adele's voice grows more powerful.

genres.name: Pussy Riot in the cathedral

place.name: Moscow, Cathedral of Christ the Saviour

genres.text: On 21 February 2012, five members of the Russian punk group Pussy Riot, in coloured balaclavas, jumped in front of the altar of a cathedral in Moscow. Within a minute they were led away. With their punk prayer they protested against President Putin. Three women were sentenced to two years in prison in August. The case became world news and showed that punk could still be dangerous to those in power.

genres.name: The Common Linnets: Calm After the Storm
genres.text: On 10 May 2014, Ilse DeLange with The Common Linnets came second at the Eurovision Song Contest in Copenhagen, the best Dutch result since Teach-In in 1975. DeLange co-wrote Calm After the Storm, a quiet country song without show or dancers. The song became a hit in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany. Since the 1990s, DeLange had shown that a Dutch woman singer could convincingly make American country.
genres.listen: Listen to the two voices of DeLange and Waylon in harmony, with acoustic guitars: country as you expect it in Nashville.

genres.name: Taylor Swift leaves Spotify
genres.text: On 3 November 2014, Taylor Swift removed all her music from Spotify, a week after her album 1989. She felt that music should not be free and that artists earned too little from streaming. In June 2015 she wrote an open letter to Apple, which did not want to pay anything during a trial period. Apple changed course within a day. In this way a pop star showed how much power she had.
genres.listen: In Shake It Off, listen to the horns and the handclaps: pure pop, a clear step away from her country past.

genres.name: Björk on who made the beats
genres.text: In January 2015, Björk said in an interview with the music site Pitchfork that she had made about eighty per cent of the beats herself for her 2001 album Vespertine. Yet the electronic duo Matmos, who had contributed, often got the credit for it. She said that women who work with men have to explain again and again what they did themselves. The interview was widely shared and discussed.

genres.name: Beyoncé: Lemonade
genres.text: On 23 April 2016, Lemonade by Beyoncé was released, together with a film of about an hour: a visual album. Beyoncé contributed to the direction, the imagery and the concept. The music ranges from blues and country to rock and hip-hop. The album is about infidelity, but also about Black women, their mothers and grandmothers, and the history of the South. She performed the closing song Formation earlier that year at the Super Bowl half-time show.

genres.name: Kesha: Praying
genres.text: In 2014, the singer Kesha sued her producer Dr. Luke for abuse and wanted to be released from her contract. The judge refused: she had to keep making records at his label. On 6 July 2017 she released Praying, a ballad about survival. A few months later the MeToo movement began, in which women around the world spoke about harassment and abuse. In the music industry, too, many stories came out.
genres.listen: Praying begins with only piano and voice. Listen to how Kesha reaches a very high note at the end, like a victory.

genres.name: Cardi B: Bodak Yellow
genres.text: On 25 September 2017, Bodak Yellow by Cardi B from the Bronx was at number one in America. It was the first time since Lauryn Hill in 1998 that a female rapper reached the top without help from others. Cardi B had become known through Instagram and a reality series. She rapped about money and success, and spoke openly about her past. In this way she became one of the biggest rappers of her time.

genres.name: Two per cent producers
genres.text: On 25 January 2018, the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative of an American university published a study of the 600 most popular songs from 2012 to 2017. Women were about a fifth of the artists, one in eight songwriters and only two per cent of the producers. Three days later the head of the Grammys said that women should step up more. After much criticism he announced that he would leave in 2019.

genres.name: Billie Eilish: bad guy
genres.text: On 29 March 2019, the debut album by Billie Eilish was released, recorded with her brother Finneas in his bedroom in the family home, without a big studio. bad guy became a number one in America, and in 2020 she won the four most important Grammys at once. With a laptop and a good microphone, someone can make a complete record at home. Whether that gives women more opportunities, the figures still have to show.
genres.listen: Listen to the whispered vocals, the deep synthesizer bass and the finger snap. A hit without a sing-along chorus, which turns into a slow section at the end.

genres.name: Running Up That Hill after 37 years
genres.text: In the summer of 2022, Running Up That Hill by Kate Bush was heard in the Netflix series Stranger Things. Millions of young people discovered the song through streaming services and TikTok. On 17 June 2022 it was at number one in Great Britain, 37 years after its first release; in 1985 it had got no further than number three. Kate Bush, who had written and produced it herself, earned from it again.
